# Introduction

This report replicates all the figures of the rerandomization simulation report, but using the fingerprint simulation where we are generating new data with each iteration.

Missing datasets:

```{r}
missing_sets
```


# How do the simulation estimated SEs compare to the actual simulation SE?

For each scenario, we can calculate true standard errors (SEs) for each method by taking the standard deviation of the point estimates across all simulation trials.
Each simulation iteration also gives an estimated standard error along with point estimate for each method.
We can then check to see if the average of the estimated standard errors (across iterations) correspond to the true standard error.
This tells us whether our estimated standard errors are accurately capturing uncertainty--in this case capturing superpopulation uncertainty when there is no treatment variation.

In short, within simulation scenario and for each method, we can compare the average estimated SE to the standard deviation of point estimates.
In the plot below we show the distribution of ratios of $E[\widehat{SE}] / SE$ across the studies, for each method.
<!--In the figure below, each dot represents the outcome for a single study.-->

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
meth_dat <- meth_dat %>%
  mutate( SE_ratio = ESEhat / SE )

ggplot( meth_dat, aes( method, SE_ratio ) ) +
  geom_boxplot( outliers=FALSE, col="darkgrey", fill = "grey" ) +
  geom_jitter( width=0.1, height=0, size=0.3 ) +
  coord_flip() +
  geom_hline( yintercept = 1, col="red" ) +
  scale_y_log10( labels = scales::percent_format(scale = 100),
                 breaks = c( 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 0.7, 1, 1.5 ) ) +
  labs( title = "Ratio of estimated SE to true SE by method",
        x = "", y = "Estimated SE / True SE" )

if ( FALSE ) {
 # Alternative plot
  ggplot( meth_dat, aes( SE, ESEhat ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ method ) +
  geom_point( alpha=0.5, size=0.5) +
  coord_fixed() +
  geom_abline( slope=1, intercept=0, lty=2 )
}
```

Some methods do not have standard errors for some scenarios (if there are too few degrees of freedom or there are too few clusters in some blocks), so they are not in the above plot--note how some boxes have fewer points.
For many methods, the average estimated SEs are generally close (well within 50%) of the true SEs.

Note the FI CRVE outliers: cluster robust standard errors can give extremely low values in some contexts.
We apparently see it here.
Our simulation should be able to show us whether this happens regularly or not in the context we are exploring.

For the record, the outlier points that are 50% or less than expected are the following:

```{r}
meth_dat %>%
  #filter( method == "LRicw-FIcw-crve" ) %>%
  dplyr::filter( ESEhat / SE < 0.5  ) %>%
  dplyr::select( method, UniqueID, SE, ESEhat, sdSEhat ) %>%
  arrange( method ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```

Some methods do not provide estimated standard errors for some of the study designs explored.
Counts of the methods with and without standard errors are below.

```{r}
emp = empirical_estimates %>% 
  group_by( method ) %>%
  summarize( num_emp = sum( !is.na( ATE_hat ) ),
             num_emp_SE = sum( !is.na( SE_hat ) ) ) 
emp
  
meth_dat %>%
  group_by( method ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
             SE_def = sum( !is.na( SE ) ),
             ESEhat_def = sum( !is.na( ESEhat ) ) ) %>%
  left_join( emp, by="method" ) %>%
  arrange( desc( ESEhat_def ), method ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

Here `num_emp` is the number of empirical (original) defined ATE estimates across the set of studies.



# How do the estimated SEs for the real data compare to the true simulation SEs?

For the most part, the average estimated SEs tend to be fairly close to the estimated _true_ SEs.
Below, we compare the estimates we got on the original empirical data to these permutaton-based true SEs.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}

mm <- meth_dat  %>%
  dplyr::select( -weight, -biased ) %>%
  left_join( empirical_estimates, 
             by=c( "Collection", "UniqueID", "Covariates", "method" ) )

mm <- mm %>%
  filter( Covariates == "best" )

ggplot( mm, aes( SE_hat, SE ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ method, nrow=3 ) +
  geom_point( alpha=0.5, size=0.5 ) +
  coord_fixed() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  geom_abline( slope=1, intercept=0, lty=2 ) +
  labs( x = "Estimated SE from empirical data",
        y = "True SE from simulation" ) +
  expand_limits(x = 0, y = 0)
```

We do see some outliers, where the true SE is way higher or way lower than what we estimated.  We filter to those studies where this occurred, showing all studies where the estimated SE is more than 50% larger than the true SE or less than 70% of the true SE:

```{r}
m2 <- mm %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter( SE > 1.5 * SE_hat | SE < 0.7*SE_hat ) %>%
  arrange( desc( SE_hat ) ) %>%
  dplyr::select( Collection, UniqueID, method, SE_hat, SE ) %>%
  mutate( off_by = SE / SE_hat ) %>%
  arrange( -off_by )

m2 %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```

`off_by` is $SE / \widehat{SE}$.


Some stats on the studies that are responsible:

```{r}
m2 %>%
  group_by( UniqueID ) %>%
  summarise( num_show = n() ) %>%
  left_join( studies, by="UniqueID" ) %>%
  dplyr::select( UniqueID, Collection, num_show, n, J, Jcv, Jbar, cons_df ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```

For the matched pairs design (TRIAD Scale Up), we often got an estimated SE that was way too small.
`jg_crt_63` is almost a matched pairs experiment (Jbar of 2.11), and shows similar issues.

# How do the actual ranges we saw compare to the ranges we get from the simulation?

For each study, we can look at the actual range of ATEs from the empirical data (red dot) vs. the ranges we get from the permutations (the boxplot).
The boxplot shows what kinds of ranges we would "naturally" see when there is no treatment effect or treatment variation.

```{r}
if ( FALSE ) {
  range_dat %>%
    filter( Estimand == "Overall" ) %>%
    group_by( UniqueID ) %>%
    summarise( sdRange = sd( rangeATE ),
               sdRatio = sd( ratioSE ) ) %>%
    knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
}

emp_dat <- empirical_estimates %>%
  group_by( UniqueID, Collection ) %>%
  summarise( rangeATE = max( ATE_hat, na.rm=TRUE ) - min( ATE_hat, na.rm=TRUE ),
             ratioSE = max( SE_hat, na.rm=TRUE ) / min( SE_hat, na.rm=TRUE ),
             .groups = "drop" )

range_dat <- range_dat %>%
  dplyr::filter( weight == "Overall" )

# Plot the ranges of ATE estimates (over all estimators)
ggplot( range_dat, aes( UniqueID, rangeATE ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ Collection, scales="free_y" ) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point( data=emp_dat, color="red" ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs( x = "", y = "Range of ATE estimates across methods",
        caption = "Red dot is the empirical range of ATE estimates" )
```


The red dots generally lie in the range of the boxplots; this means the range we saw in our empirical data is entirely consistent with the ranges we would see if there were no treatment effect, or variation in treatment effect, whatsoever.
Our observed range, therefore, does not appear to be driven by the estimators targeting different estimands.

To quantify this, we can calculate the percent of studies where the empirical range is outside the 90% interval of the simulated ranges:

```{r}
tmp <- range_dat %>%
  group_by(Collection, UniqueID) %>%
  summarise(
    mn_range = mean(rangeATE),
    q95 = quantile(rangeATE, 0.95),
    q05 = quantile(rangeATE, 0.05),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  left_join(emp_dat, by = c("Collection", "UniqueID")) %>%
  mutate(
    below05 = rangeATE < q05,
    above95 = rangeATE > q95,
    outside_90 = below05 | above95
  )

test <- tmp %>%
  group_by(Collection) %>%
  summarise(
    per_below_05 = mean(below05) * 100,
    per_above_95 = mean(above95) * 100,
    percent_outside_90 = mean(outside_90) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )
tov <- tmp %>%
      summarise(
        Collection = "Overall",
        per_below_05 = mean(below05) * 100,
        per_above_95 = mean(above95) * 100,
        percent_outside_90 = mean(outside_90) * 100
      )

bind_rows( test, tov ) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 0)

```


We can look at the range of ATE estimates vs size of study (number of clusters).
The empirical are plotted as dots on the lines.


```{r}
rr <- range_dat %>%
  left_join( studies, by=c( "Collection", "UniqueID" ) )
rr_emp = filter( rr, runID == "empirical" )

emp_dat_full <- left_join( emp_dat, studies, by=c( "Collection", "UniqueID" ) )

ggplot( rr, aes( n, rangeATE, color=Collection, group=UniqueID ) ) +
  geom_boxplot( outliers = FALSE ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ Collection ) +
  geom_point( data=emp_dat_full, color="black" ) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs( x = "Number of clusters",
        y = "Range of ATE estimates",
        title = "Range of ATE estimates by number of clusters" )
```

Note: When there are multiple outcomes for the same study, these lines are overplotted.




# How do the actual SE-hat ratios compare to what we get from simulation?

We next look at how much the ratio of the max to min estimated standard errors vary across the permutations, and compare that to the ratios from the empirical data.

TODO: Look at the studies with big ranges and big estimated ranges.  Do they correspond to the empirical results and identified studies in the "flashcard report"?  Do a cross check to see if the "weird studies" there are captured here, and vice-versa.  (We noticed some discrepancies and need to follow up.)


```{r}
range_dat %>%
  ggplot( aes( UniqueID, ratioSE ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ Collection, scales="free_y" ) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point( data=emp_dat, color="red" ) +
  coord_flip() +
    scale_y_log10( breaks=c(1,2,3,4,5),
                 labels = scales::percent_format(scale = 100) ) +
  labs( title = "Variation in Ratio of maxSE to minSE" )
```

For many studies, the ratio is in line with our simulation.
For others, we see ratios well outside of what we would expect.
In particular, there are several studies where the ratio is far smaller than the simulation would suggest we would find.

The structure of the study seems to drive the ratio in many cases.
jg_crt_31, for example, nearly always has a very large ratio, even though empirically we see a small ratio.


```{r}
tmp <- range_dat %>%
  group_by(Collection, UniqueID) %>%
  summarise(
    mn_range = mean(ratioSE),
    q95 = quantile(ratioSE, 0.95),
    q05 = quantile(ratioSE, 0.05),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  left_join(emp_dat, by = c("Collection", "UniqueID")) %>%
  mutate(
    below05 = ratioSE < q05,
    above95 = ratioSE > q95,
    outside_90 = below05 | above95
  )

tmp %>%
  group_by(Collection) %>%
  summarise(
    per_below_05 = mean(below05) * 100,
    per_above_95 = mean(above95) * 100,
    percent_outside_90 = mean(outside_90) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  bind_rows(
    tmp %>%
      summarise(
        Collection = "Overall",
        per_below_05 = mean(below05) * 100,
        per_above_95 = mean(above95) * 100,
        percent_outside_90 = mean(outside_90) * 100
      )
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 0)
```

Overall, we are seeing more empirical values in the tails of the ranges--overall 23% of the studies have ratios in the 5% tails (10% total) of the simulated ranges.


Generally we see our simulation ratios are failing to capture what ratios we are seeing in practice much of the time.

# Examining estimator performance

In the following I continue to examine how the different estimators perform, relative to the other estimators.


## Question 1: Do some methods have higher true standard errors than other methods?

First we compare standard errors of methods by looking at the ratio of the true SE vs. median true SE within study, and then making a boxplot

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
meth_dat <- meth_dat %>%
  group_by( UniqueID ) %>%
  mutate( SE_ratio = SE / median( SE, na.rm=TRUE ) ) %>%
  ungroup()

ggplot( meth_dat, aes( method, SE_ratio ) ) +
  geom_boxplot( outliers=FALSE, fill="grey", col="darkgrey" ) +
  geom_jitter( width = 0.2, height=0, size=0.5 ) + 
  coord_flip() +
  geom_hline( yintercept = 1, col="red" ) +
  labs( title = "relative SE to methods in study" )
```

Discussion: All the methods have a SE ratio that is, at the median, the same as the other methods.  This suggests that the methods all have the same overall performance across datasets, on average.
That said, some methods have long right tails, meaning there are some studies where their true SEs are more than 50% larger than the median performing method.
Other methods have studies where they are notable more stable than other methods, by even 50% or more.


We can organize these same values by study to see if some studies naturally lead to bigger ranges of true SE:

```{r}
ggplot( meth_dat, aes( UniqueID, SE_ratio ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ Collection, scales="free_y" ) +
  geom_boxplot( outliers=FALSE, fill="grey", col="darkgrey" ) +
geom_jitter( width = 0.2, height=0, size=0.5 ) + 
  geom_hline( yintercept = 1, col="red" ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs( title = "relative SE to methods in study", x="" )
```


The second plot shows that some studies indeed have a wider range of true SEs than other studies.  For example, some estimators in `jg_crt_2` have larger SEs and some have smaller SEs.  By contrast, almost everyone in `Beacon_S8TGPA` have the same true SE (note the very narrow boxplot).
We also see clustering --- this is partly due to some estimators being virtually identical.

We can then make a histogram of the ratios of the largest to smallest _true_ SE by study.
This is the "true" version of our main ratio plot in the main paper.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.height=3}
true_se <- meth_dat %>% 
  group_by( UniqueID ) %>%
  summarise( true_rat = max( SE ) / min( SE ) )

ggplot( true_se, aes( true_rat ) ) +
  geom_dotplot( method = "histodot", binwidth = 0.05 ) +
  labs( title = "Ratio of highest to lowest true SE by study" )
```

These ratios are all inflated by simulation error (we do not fully know the true SEs).
That said, we are seeing many large ratios suggesting that for many studies we really would expect the SEs to vary substantially based on estimator choice. 



```{r}

rg_emp <- left_join( range_dat, true_se,
                     by=c( "UniqueID" ) )
ggplot( rg_emp, aes( ratioSE, true_rat ) ) +
  geom_point( alpha=0.5, size=0.5 ) +
  coord_fixed() +
  geom_abline( slope=1, intercept=0, lty=2 ) +
  labs( x = "Estimated SE ratio",
        y = "True SE ratio",
        title = "Estimated vs True SE ratio by study" )
```

The above plot shows how the true ratio is very different from the max/min ratio of the estimated SEs for many of our studies.
It also shows how the estimated ratios can be very much larger than the true ones.

We can look at it in light of the figure from the main paper:

```{r}
#ggplot( rg_emp, aes( true_rat ) ) +
#  geom_density( data=range_dat, aes( x=ratioSE ), 
#                fill="grey", alpha=0.5, adjust=0.5 ) +
#  geom_dotplot( method = "histodot", binwidth = 0.01 ) +
#  labs( title = "Ratio of highest to lowest true SE by study" )
rg_L <- rg_emp %>%
  pivot_longer( cols = c( ratioSE, true_rat ),
                names_to = "type", values_to = "ratioSE" )
ggplot( rg_L, aes( ratioSE, fill=type ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ type, ncol=1 ) +
  #geom_dotplot( method = "histodot", binwidth = 0.025 ) +
  geom_density() + 
  labs( title = "Ratio of highest to lowest true SE by study" )

```

In the above we see the clear contraction of the ratios when we look at _true_ SE ratios vs _estimated_ SE ratios.

# Addendum: Modeling to understand variation

**NOTE: This part is rough work in progress**

The true SEs are estimated with error, across only 20 simulation replicates.
We can account for this uncertainty by fitting a model where we regress $log( \widehat{ATE}^2 )$ onto a random effect for study, method, and study by method.

The average error is essentially the log of the estimated SE.
Note that 
$$ SE = E[ (\widehat{ATE}-E[ATE])^2 ] .$$
We then plug in $E[ATE]$ to get individual permutation estimates of the standard error:
$$ err = (\widehat{ATE} - \frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^R \widehat{ATE}_r)^2$$
where $R$ is the number of permutations.
Then regressing the log of these onto method and study will let us know if some methods have systematically higher or lower SEs than others, controlling for study.
We include interactions to allow these differences to be different for some studies.

```{r}
library( lme4 )
simdat <- simdat %>%
  group_by( UniqueID, method ) %>%
  mutate( err = log( ( ATE_hat - mean(ATE_hat) )^2 ) ) %>%
  ungroup()
#summary( simdat$err )
M <- lmer( err ~ 1 + (1|method) + (1|UniqueID) + (1|method:UniqueID), data=simdat )
arm::display( M )

VarCorr(M)
#rr <- ranef(M)
#rr$`method:UniqueID`
```

This shows we are seeing variation by method in terms of the log of the squared error--i.e., some methods have larger errors than other methods.




## Question 2: Do some methods have more trouble estimating their standard error?


For each estimator in each study, we can calculate $sd( \widehat{SE} ) / SE$.  We then make boxplots of those values for each study.

```{r, warning=FALSE}
meth_dat <- meth_dat %>%
  mutate( sdSEhat_ratio = sdSEhat / SE )
ggplot( meth_dat, aes( UniqueID, sdSEhat_ratio ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ Collection, scales="free_y" ) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip( ylim=c(0.00001,1 ) ) +
    scale_y_log10() +
  
  labs( title = "sd( SE-hat ) / SE for estimators within study" )
```

These standard deviations can be generally quite small (note the log scale)--this suggests most standard errors are precisely estimated, and that the estimates are very stable across differently generated datasets.

We can look at these relative to the overall median SE, to turn them all into ratios.

```{r, warning=FALSE}
meth_dat <- meth_dat %>%
  group_by( UniqueID ) %>%
  mutate( relSE = sdSEhat / median( SE, na.rm=TRUE ) ) %>%
  ungroup()

# sd( SE-hat ) across study
ggplot( meth_dat, aes( UniqueID, relSE ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ Collection, scales="free_y" ) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip( ylim=c(0.0001,1 ) ) +
    scale_y_log10() +
  geom_hline( yintercept = 0.05, col="red" ) +
  labs( title = "sd( SE-hat ) / median(SE-hat) for estimators within study",
        caption = "Red line at 0.05" )
```

Interestingly, many of the $sd( \widehat{SE} )$ values are extremely stable; the standard deviations are virtually zero.
The most stable we see are the following:

```{r}
meth_dat %>%
  arrange( relSE ) %>%
  dplyr::select( UniqueID, method, SE, ESEhat, sdSEhat, relSE ) %>%
  slice_head( n = 20 ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 3 )
```

We can see if some estimators are more stable than others:

```{r, warning=FALSE}
ggplot( meth_dat, aes( method, relSE ) ) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip( ylim=c(0.0001,1 ) ) +
    scale_y_log10() +
  geom_hline( yintercept = c( 0.05, 0.1), col="red" ) +
  labs( title = "sd( SE-hat ) / median(SE-hat) for estimators across studies",
        caption = "red line at 0.05 and 0.10; log scale x-axis!" )
```

Indeed some are.  Note that if a box edge hits the 0.10 line, then more than 25% of the studies have a $sd( \widehat{SE} )$ that is more than 10% of the median true SE.

# Digging into TRIADScale-up_rema2

We can look at `TRIADScale-up_rema2`.


## How do the point estimates correlate? 

Here we look at how point estimates of the different methods correlate with other point estimates across the replicates.
Each point corresponds to two estimators applied to a single shared dataset.
We are looking at all of the estimators that are unique, several estimators were dropped because they are not defined for this data set.

```{r, warning=FALSE}
triad <- filter( simdat, UniqueID == "TRIADScale-up_rema2",
                 Covariates == "best" ) %>%
  dplyr::select( -UniqueID, -Covariates, -Collection )

triad_emp = triad %>%
  dplyr::filter( runID == "empirical" )
triad <- triad %>%
  dplyr::filter( runID != "empirical" )


tt <- triad %>%
  dplyr::filter( method %in% core.methods, !is.na( ATE_hat ) ) %>%
  dplyr::select( runID, method, ATE_hat ) %>%
  pivot_wider( names_from = method, values_from = ATE_hat )



plot( tt[,-1] )

```

## How do the estimated SEs look?

We look at the estimated standard errors across the simulations. We are seeing some estimators reliabily give very different standard error estimates.

The red lines showed the true standard error across the replicates.
The histogram shows the range of estimated standard errors.
Some of the estimators are giving systematically wrong standard errors that do not match the true standard error.

This could be due to the randomness of the blocks, which the estimators do not take into account---they are assuming there is no block variation.
That said, there is no block treatment variation---this is just randomness of the block intercepts.


```{r}

ttt <- filter( triad, !is.na( SE_hat ) )

trueSE <- triad %>% 
  group_by( method ) %>%
  summarise( trueSE = sd( ATE_hat, na.rm=TRUE ) ) %>%
  filter( method %in% ttt$method )

ggplot( ttt, aes( SE_hat ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~method ) +
#  geom_dotplot( method="histodot", binwidth = 0.005 ) +
  geom_histogram() +
  geom_vline( data=trueSE, aes( xintercept = trueSE ), col="red" ) +
  theme(panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA))


#triad %>% 
#  group_by( runID ) %>%
#  filter( !is.na( SE_hat ) ) %>%
#  summarise( SE_ratio = max( SE_hat ) / min( SE_hat ) ) %>%
#  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )

if ( FALSE ) {
  tt <- triad %>%
  dplyr::filter(method %in% core.methods.se) %>%
  dplyr::select(runID, method, SE_hat) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = method, values_from = SE_hat) %>%
  dplyr::select(where(~ !all(is.na(.))))
}

```

And how do the estimators perform?

```{r}
triad %>% group_by( method ) %>%
  summarise( SE = sd( ATE_hat ),
             ESEhat = mean( SE_hat ),
             sdSEhat = sd( SE_hat ),
             cal = ESEhat / SE ) %>%
  arrange( -sdSEhat ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 3 )
```


# Digging into jg_crt_63

We can look at `jg_crt_63`, the other "nearly a matched pair" scenario:


## How do the point estimates correlate? 

```{r}
triad <- filter( simdat, UniqueID == "jg_crt_63",
                 Covariates == "best" ) %>%
  dplyr::select( -UniqueID, -Covariates, -Collection )

triad_emp = triad %>%
  dplyr::filter( runID == "empirical" )
triad <- triad %>%
  dplyr::filter( runID != "empirical" )

tt <- triad %>%
  dplyr::filter( method %in% core.methods, !is.na( ATE_hat ) ) %>%
  dplyr::select( runID, method, ATE_hat ) %>%
  pivot_wider( names_from = method, values_from = ATE_hat )



plot( tt[,-1] )

```

## How do the estimated SEs work?
```{r}

ttt <- filter( triad, !is.na( SE_hat ) )

trueSE <- triad %>% 
  group_by( method ) %>%
  summarise( trueSE = sd( ATE_hat, na.rm=TRUE ) ) %>%
  filter( method %in% ttt$method )

ggplot( ttt, aes( SE_hat ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~method ) +
#  geom_dotplot( method="histodot", binwidth = 0.005 ) +
  geom_histogram() +
  geom_vline( data=trueSE, aes( xintercept = trueSE ), col="red" ) +
  theme(panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA))


if ( FALSE ) {
  triad %>% 
  group_by( runID ) %>%
  filter( !is.na( SE_hat ) ) %>%
  summarise( SE_ratio = max( SE_hat ) / min( SE_hat ) ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )


tt <- triad %>%
  dplyr::filter(method %in% core.methods.se) %>%
  dplyr::select(runID, method, SE_hat) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = method, values_from = SE_hat) %>%
  dplyr::select(where(~ !all(is.na(.))))

}

```

## And how do the estimators perform?

```{r}
triad %>% group_by( method ) %>%
  summarise( SE = sd( ATE_hat ),
             ESEhat = mean( SE_hat ),
             sdSEhat = sd( SE_hat ),
             cal = ESEhat / SE ) %>%
  arrange( -sdSEhat ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 3 )
```










# Digging into jg_crt_23

We can look at `jg_crt_23`, one of the studies that was not remarkable in terms of poor performance of anything.


## How do the point estimates correlate? 

```{r}
triad <- filter( simdat, UniqueID == "jg_crt_23",
                 Covariates == "best" ) %>%
  dplyr::select( -UniqueID, -Covariates, -Collection )

triad_emp = triad %>%
  dplyr::filter( runID == "empirical" )
triad <- triad %>%
  dplyr::filter( runID != "empirical" )

tt <- triad %>%
  dplyr::filter( method %in% core.methods, !is.na( ATE_hat ) ) %>%
  dplyr::select( runID, method, ATE_hat ) %>%
  pivot_wider( names_from = method, values_from = ATE_hat )

plot( tt[,-1] )

```

## How do the estimated SEs work?
```{r}

ttt <- filter( triad, !is.na( SE_hat ) )

trueSE <- triad %>% 
  group_by( method ) %>%
  summarise( trueSE = sd( ATE_hat, na.rm=TRUE ) ) %>%
  filter( method %in% ttt$method )

ggplot( ttt, aes( SE_hat ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~method ) +
  geom_histogram() +
  geom_vline( data=trueSE, aes( xintercept = trueSE ), col="red" ) +
  theme(panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA))

```

## And how do the estimators perform?

```{r}
triad %>% group_by( method ) %>%
  summarise( SE = sd( ATE_hat ),
             ESEhat = mean( SE_hat ),
             sdSEhat = sd( SE_hat ),
             cal = ESEhat / SE ) %>%
  arrange( -sdSEhat ) %>%
```
